entities.name: Gwenwynwyn
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Gwenwynwyn ab Owain Cyfeiliog (died 1216) was a pivotal prince of Powys Wenwynwyn in eastern Wales, whose turbulent reign from 1195 to 1216 marked a critical phase in the Anglo-Welsh struggles for regional dominance. Operating from his power base in southern Powys, he was one of the last native Welsh rulers to mount a significant, albeit ultimately unsuccessful, challenge to the burgeoning hegemony of Llywelyn ab Iorwerth (Llywelyn the Great) of Gwynedd. His fluctuating alliances with the English Crown, particularly King John, and his persistent rivalry with Llywelyn shaped the political landscape of Wales in the early 13th century, delaying the complete consolidation of Welsh power under Gwynedd for a time.

Throughout his rule, Gwenwynwyn engaged in a complex and often contradictory diplomatic and military strategy. He frequently sought English protection against Llywelyn, paying homage to King John in 1208 and receiving lands in return, yet he also periodically rebelled against English authority, leading to the destruction of his principal castle at Mathrafal in 1212. His military campaigns often aimed to expand his territory eastward into the Welsh Marches or to assert control over neighboring Welsh lordships, often clashing directly with Llywelyn's forces. These conflicts, though not always decisive, prevented a unified Welsh front against English encroachment during a crucial period of consolidation for the Principality of Gwynedd.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Gwenwynwyn's resistance to Llywelyn the Great and his complex relationship with the English Crown profoundly shaped the political landscape of Wales in the early 13th century, delaying Welsh unification and influencing the eventual English conquest of the region.
